hook.line: In a review, the difference between "just any café" and "not just any café" is the difference between a shrug and a compliment. One small word after the noun does it.

examples.en: It was just an ordinary Tuesday.

examples.es: Era una tarde cualquiera en el café.
examples.en: It was just an ordinary afternoon at the café.
Pass me any book. (to a friend)
One ordinary night, Hernando turned up.

examples.es: Cualquier día de estos te llamo.
examples.en: I'll call you one of these days. (to a friend)

rule:
After the noun, *cualquiera* means "ordinary", "just any old": *un martes cualquiera*. Add *no* and you make it special: *No es una película cualquiera.* = it isn't just any film.

Before the noun, it shrinks to *cualquier* and means "any, whichever": *cualquier día de estos*.

So position changes the meaning. After the noun it keeps the full form, *cualquiera*, for masculine and feminine alike.

Never put the long form before a noun: not *cualquiera persona*.
smallPrint: Teachers call *cualquier* before a noun an indefinite adjective that drops its ending; the full form after the noun is a different, more descriptive use.
